rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 - survey of 131 drip-adopter households in Pokharathok village (Palpa, Nepal) in 2003 using unstructured questionnaires, random-spot observation of time use, focus groups and benefit-cost analysis. Q2: Section 3.2 - before drip only 3% of households produced vegetables and 72% of farmers ate no vegetables at meals; after intervention 100% of drip users consumed vegetables with meals; about 30% bought milking cows from vegetable income so milk entered meals; Table 2 - two-thirds of women agreed drip brought changes in daily vegetable intake; Conclusion states drip had a significant positive impact on family food and nutritional intake. Q4: Section 3.3 / Table 5 - vegetable production per household (510 kg), gross income (~US$67) and women's access to and control of cash (92% had no income before) are measured as the pathway to improved food availability (Section 3.2 says improvement is in part because of women's access to income). Q6: Sections 2 and 3.2 - effect reported across a whole village community of 131 adopting households, a 'massive boom' in regional vegetable production. Q7: Section 3.3 - authors state that access to water is the key factor and that market sustenance (IDE-established collection centres) and credit access are also crucial; Conclusion - benefits realised when the technology is offered within a favourable institutional environment; Section 3.4 - expansion difficult where water is scarce. Q8: Conclusion - degree to which outside institutional support made the technology viable is not known; long-term sustainability of the livelihood questionable; returns depend on market prices.
rows.notes: Food/nutrition result is before-after recall by adopters with no non-adopter control group. Q3 answered no because both the diet figures (from group discussions) and the Table 2 perception statement are self-reports from the same respondents, not independent methods; the random-spot observation measured labour, not diet. Q6 is a village-level survey rather than a scheme or district; a stricter reader might answer no. Q9: only percentages reported, no SD/CI/range for the dietary result. The 'frequency of vegetable intake 9 to 14 per week' and '50% income increase' figures are from Gurung (2000), not own results.

rows.evidence: Q1: Section 2 - own household survey of 131 adopters, focus groups and BCA in one Nepali village. Q2: Section 3.3 / Table 5 - average gross household income about US$67 from a 0.013 ha plot; NPV US$16.1, BCR 2.4, IRR 37.9%, payback 1.6 years; Section 3.2 - 92% of women had no income source before adoption and now have access and control; Table 2 - 84% agreed drip generates more income than other livelihood options; Dalits and de facto female-headed households reported highest gains (Box 1 case); Section 3.4 - authors conclude the technology carries huge potential for poverty reduction. Q4: Table 5 / Section 3.3 - production (510 kg), revenue, kit cost (~US$13), labour days, rent and input costs measured as the pathway to net income. Q6: Sections 2-3 - income effects reported across a village community of 131 households, with village-level market collection centres and a group fund exceeding NRs 100,000. Q7: Section 3.3 - states that without a reliable, sustained output market income generation is not possible; access to water is the key factor; credit access crucial (lack of capital the main non-adoption constraint, Table 7); Conclusion - favourable institutional environment needed. Q8: Conclusion - returns depend on market prices and number of adopters; viability without outside institutional support unknown; Section 3.3 - all respondents owned land and used family labour so BCA assumptions of opportunity cost may not reflect landless farmers; single village chosen for its high number of adopters.
rows.notes: The claim passage concerns income and poverty, which the study addresses with its own data; the 'social_cohesion' label is also partly supported (women's self-help saving-credit groups, Dalits socialising) but rated on the passage. Q3 answered no: the BCA is computed from survey-reported costs and revenues and the perception statements come from the same respondents, so they are not independent methods. The '>50% increase in mean income' figure is from Gurung (2000), not an own result. No control group. Q9: no SD/CI/range on income or BCA outputs (the rent range is an input, not result dispersion).

notes: Document is IWMI Working Paper 87 (Upadhyay, Samad, Giordano 2005) though cited as 2004. Tables 1-7 and the reference list are rendered in a garbled font encoding and are largely unreadable; ratings rely on the numerical values restated in the body text. Study is a single-village cross-sectional adopter survey with before/after recall and no comparison group.
